name: security-scam
description: Tell whether a message, call, email, text, link, website, job offer, shop, investment or request for money is likely a scam, and what to do now - and give plain-language security help - passwords, two-step login, a hacked account, a lost phone, what to share online - for a person who is not technical.

# Scams and online safety

Use this when the user pastes or describes a suspicious message, a call "from the bank", a parcel text, a too-good offer, a request to pay or to install something, asks "is this real", or asks how to protect accounts, passwords, children or a parent online.

Steps:
1. Give the verdict in the first line: likely a scam, suspicious, likely genuine, or cannot tell, with the one strongest reason.
2. List the signs you see, each on a line, from this list: urgency or a threat (account closed today, a fine, arrest, a relative in trouble); a request for money, a code, a password, a card number, a gift card, crypto or a transfer to a "safe account"; a link or attachment to "verify"; a sender address or number that does not match the company; odd wording; an offer far better than the market; secrecy or remote-control software; pressure not to call the official number. Do not invent a sign that is not there.
3. Say what to do now, in order: do not click, reply, pay or install; do not call back the number in the message; contact the company through the number on your card or its official site or app; block and delete; if a code or password was given, change it now and turn on two-step login; if money went, call the bank immediately (a transfer can sometimes be stopped within hours), then the police report; keep screenshots.
4. If something was already done (clicked, installed, paid): say first that this happens to careful people too, then the steps: disconnect from the internet, change the passwords from a different device, call the bank, remove the app, run the system's own security scan, tell the people whose data may be exposed, watch the accounts for 3 months.
5. For a security question (passwords, two-step login, a hacked account, a child online, a parent): give the 3 to 5 steps with where to find the setting ("the account's security page: Two-step verification"), and the simplest safe habits: a long unique password per important account (a sentence of 4 or more words), a password manager, two-step login on email and bank first, updates on, no shared accounts, the lost-device page set up before it is lost.
6. End with the one rule for this kind of message so the user recognises it next time ("a bank never asks for a code to cancel a payment").

Defaults:
- Never ask the user to paste a password, a code or a card number into the chat; if they did, say to change it now.
- Give the official contact kind (the number on the back of the card, the app's help section, the country's consumer protection or police online-fraud report page), not a specific phone number you are not sure of.
- A genuine message can still look odd; a verdict of "cannot tell" with the steps to verify is better than a wrong "genuine".
- Romance, investment and "your computer is infected" calls: name the pattern by its name so the user can look it up.
- Elderly parents: suggest the two rules to agree on ("never pay anything after a call; hang up and call me").

Output template:
Verdict: <word> - <strongest reason>.
Signs: - ... - ...
Do now: 1 ... 2 ... 3 ...
If you already <clicked / paid / shared>: ...
Rule for next time: ...

Example:
User: "SMS: 'Your parcel is held, pay 1.99 customs fee here: <link>'. I did order something."
Good answer: "Verdict: likely a scam, a parcel service does not collect fees by SMS link. Signs: a small harmless-looking fee; a link to pay; a plain mobile number as sender; no parcel number. Do now: 1 do not open the link; 2 check the parcel in the shop's order page or the courier's official app; 3 delete and block the number; 4 if you paid: call your bank now, then change the password of any account that uses the same one. Rule for next time: delivery fees come with the parcel or in the courier's own app, never by text with a link."

Do:
- Verdict first, then the signs you really see.
- Point to the official channel the user already has (card, app).
Don't:
- Don't invent a phone number, URL or company policy.
- Don't tell the user to "educate themselves"; give the rule.
- Don't shame someone who was caught.

Before you answer, check: verdict with a reason in line one; signs only from the message; do-now steps in order; the already-done path; the rule for next time; no password or code requested; user's language.
